moves.spoken: The Accelerated Dragon — Black will fianchetto and get quick, harmonious development.
The bishop heads to the long diagonal; White, meanwhile, is about to trade on c6.
That trade is already a slight inaccuracy: recapturing toward the centre opens the b-file and prepares the d5 break.
The fianchetto completed — the open b-file and a coming d5 are the source of Black's play.
White offers a trade of dark-squared bishops on the long diagonal — do we allow it?
Developing the knight to f6 declines the trade cleanly; the tempting e5 would be bad, weakening the d6 square.
f3 is the kind of move players make on autopilot, but it is incredibly weakening.
Castle and finish development.
The bishop to c4 walks straight into a break Black should be playing automatically.
d5 — occupying the centre and challenging at once.
White will drop the bishop back; that leads to a very instructive moment.
The bishop to d3 is a genuinely good move. First order of business now: prevent White from castling.
The queen to b6 stops castling. It may not prevent it forever, but every tempo White spends dislodging the queen, Black spends expanding in the centre.
Stay flexible. There is a reason strong players warn never to play f3 — it is one of the most weakening moves on the board.
Expanding in the centre — d4 would close off the bishop's long diagonal and help him castle, so the move is e5.
Had White captured on e5, the bishop would have been pinned with devastating effect.
White wants the bishop to e3, but he is not in time — Black is ready to rampage in the centre.
e4 — and the beauty is Black can recapture with either the knight or the pawn.
Recapturing with the pawn to keep things simple, though taking with the knight was also very strong.
White's whole intention is the bishop to e3 and then castling — that is why the queen went to c1.

The knight to g4 stops the bishop reaching e3, and with the long diagonal open the bishop eyes the pawn on b2. If h3, then not only a capture on b2 hitting the queen, but even a check on f2 with mate to follow — you don't need the exact mate, only to trust the position.
He defends against the check on f2 — but don't forget the other set of ideas.
Simplest of all: just take on b2 and win a load of material. Call it life insurance — if the attack ever misfires, you are still up a rook.
The immediate e3 is tempting, but it blunts our own queen; better to keep those squares open for it.
When you can win a full rook, take it — the safe, clean conversion, even when a mate might be lurking.
